p.title: An Application of Data Mining Techniques to Explore Congressional Lobbying Records for Patterns in Pediatric Special Interest Expenditures Prior to the Affordable Care Act

ext.title: An Application of Data Mining Techniques to Explore Congressional Lobbying Records for Patterns in Pediatric Special Interest Expenditures Prior to the Affordable Care Act
ext.venue: Frontiers in Big Data, Data Report, vol. 1, article 3 (published 20 August 2018; received 24 April 2018; accepted 2 August 2018)
ext.document_type: Data report (methods demonstration with a short descriptive analysis; no inferential statistics)
ext.identification: None. This is a descriptive data-parsing report. It makes no causal or identification claim and does not estimate any effect of lobbying on legislation. Metadata hint confirmed (title, year, venue, DOI); full author first names taken from the byline on p.1.
ext.coverage: Full text read in one pass: the entire 19,401-character text file (408 lines, pp.1-4 including the reference list and footers). Sections 1 (Background), 2 (Data and Methodology, incl. 2.1-2.4), 3 (Analysis), 4 (Future Research), the data availability statement and references are all covered. Figures 1 and 2 are referenced in the text (organization tree; XML parsing pseudocode) but their content is not in the extracted text, so they are not described. Annotations: all 11 items in the annotation JSON were read (10 yellow highlights, 1 green highlight, all by Paul Goff, no sticky notes or typed notes). Covered text in paul_markup is paraphrased, not quoted, per the copyright rule; the exact span can be found at the page and rect coordinates in the annotation file. Topic coverage: lobbying and health legislation (yes, background and results); networks (only a passing mention of social network analysis in the background, no network analysis performed); path-finding and allocation (no); elections, campaign finance and turnout (no, the paper addresses lobbying spend only); persuasion (no); legislators as units (no, the unit is the filing); text measurement (no analysis performed; NLP and topic modeling proposed as future work in Sec. 4).
ext.research_question: Stated in Sec. 1 and Sec. 2: the paper illustrates data parsing principles for mining federal lobbying records, and shows how one might investigate trends in how pediatric health concerns enter the political environment, using Q4 2009 LDA filings made before the Affordable Care Act. No formal hypothesis is stated.
ext.theory: Not stated. The background (Sec. 1, p.1) motivates the work with a general concern about the thin empirical literature on financial lobbying influence on health legislation, and with a history of child-health advocacy. No theoretical framework or testable hypothesis is set out.
ext.data: Source: public Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) XML downloads from the US Senate Office of Public Records (Sec. 2.1, p.2). Sample period: lobbying filings submitted in Q4 2009, filtered to events dated 2009 (filings in that quarter also contained activity from 2002-2008, Sec. 2.3, p.2). Unit: the lobbying filing (XML records, each grouped by filing time). Size: about 25 XML files per quarter at roughly 1,000 lines each, more than 25,000 lines of XML in total (Sec. 2.1). Eight data frames: Filing, Issue, Entity, Org, Lobbyist, Registrant, Client, Government Entity (Sec. 2.3). Pediatric keyword search returned 35 results from the Q4 2009 frame (Sec. 2.4, p.2). Total number of filings in the quarter is not reported.
ext.method: Descriptive data engineering in Python 3.6.4: ElementTree parses the XML hierarchy; os.listdir enumerates files; a parsing loop (pseudocode in Fig. 2) converts records into Pandas data frames, with defaultdict holding a master dictionary (Sec. 2.2-2.3). Filing and Issue frames are merged, and reported dollar amounts are summed by issue code (a Pandas series grouped by code, Sec. 2.3). A search function returns every record whose Specific Issues text contains a user-supplied term; the term "pediatric" is used (Sec. 2.4). Search hits are compared with the code-level totals (Sec. 2.4). No statistical tests, models or regressions are run.
ext.scope: Population: lobbying disclosures filed under the LDA in one calendar quarter (Q4 2009), covering all issue areas, with a pediatric subset identified by keyword. Institution: US federal Congress and federal agencies (the LDA). Era: pre-ACA (2009-2010 passage). A single-quarter, single-keyword methods illustration, not a population-level or multi-year study.

key_findings.finding: Largest sum of reported lobbying dollars for Q4 2009 is filed under the umbrella code Taxation/Internal Revenue Code.
Health Issues is the second-largest umbrella code by reported dollars.
The pediatric keyword search returns 35 records from the Q4 2009 frame, spread across several umbrella codes.
key_findings.numbers: 35 hits; codes include Health Issues, Budget Appropriations, Science/Technology, Education, Disaster Planning & Emergencies, Medicare/Medicaid

key_findings.finding: Pediatric-related issues are bundled with many unrelated issues inside single filings, so dollars spent on pediatric lobbying cannot be isolated.
key_findings.numbers: not quantified; illustrated with one filing listing multiple vaccine, Medicare/Medicaid, FDA and pandemic issues together

key_findings.finding: Records are grouped by filing date, so a quarter's files include activity from earlier years.
key_findings.numbers: activity dated 2002-2008 filed in Q4 2009; a date filter restricts output to 2009 events

key_findings.finding: The XML amounts do not separate lobbying expenditures from income, and no identifier links them, so reported dollars cannot be split by type.
Expenses under a threshold are reported as a checkbox with no amount, and client income over the threshold is rounded to the nearest $10,000.
key_findings.numbers: expenses under $5,000 (checkbox); client income over $5,000 rounded to nearest $10,000

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude the public LDA system remains opaque despite searchable data and downloadable XML, and that analysis of the currency values is limited until the forms change.

measures: Sum of reported lobbying dollars by umbrella issue code (Filing + Issue merge, grouped by code)
Count of records whose Specific Issues text contains the term 'pediatric' (35)
Filing date and activity-year fields used to restrict to 2009 events
limitations: Reported dollars cannot be split into lobbying expenditures versus client income (Sec. 3, p.3).
Expenses under $5,000 are a checkbox with no amount, and client income above $5,000 is rounded to the nearest $10,000 (Sec. 3, pp.3-4).
Pediatric-related dollars cannot be isolated because related issues are bundled with unrelated issues in the same filing (Sec. 3, p.3).
Analysis covers one quarter (Q4 2009) and one search term; the paper states the term was chosen for sensitivity and specificity but does not test other terms (Sec. 2.4).
Records are grouped by filing date rather than activity date, so the sample mixes activity years (Sec. 2.3, p.2).
The paper performs no statistical analysis; the authors say deeper statistical manipulation of currency values could be assessed only after the forms change (Sec. 4, p.4).
Text-level analysis (NLP, topic modeling) is proposed for future work but not done (Sec. 4, p.4).
Total number of filings in the quarter and the denominator for the 35 hits are not reported.

[paraphrase] Python offered as a general-purpose toolbox for political researchers, clinicians and data scientists (Sec. 2).
[paraphrase] Q4 2009 chosen as a period of intense healthcare lobbying before the ACA passed (Sec. 2.1).
[paraphrase] Each quarter has about 25 congressional lobbying XML files of roughly 1,000 lines each (Sec. 2.1).
[paraphrase] ElementTree parses the hierarchical XML into root and child attributes, which are sorted into other structures (Sec. 2.2).
[paraphrase] Filings are grouped by filing time, not activity time; some Q4 2009 filings cover 2002-2008 activity (Sec. 2.3).
[paraphrase] An effective initial query needs a wide set of related search terms (Sec. 2.4).

Steinbrook, R. (2009). Lobbying, campaign contributions, and health care reform. N. Engl. J. Med. 361:e52. Cited (Sec. 1) for about $1.7 billion spent lobbying Congress and agencies on health since 2006 and for the thin empirical literature on lobbying and health legislation.

Asch, D. A., Rader, D. J., and Merchant, R. M. (2015). Mining the social mediome. Trends Mol. Med. 21, 528-529. Cited (Sec. 1) only in passing for social network analysis as an emerging data-science method in social-science settings; the paper does not use networks.

short_quotes.quote: XML files do not differentiate lobbying expenditures from income

rel.summary_md:
Harrison, Dreisbach, Basit and Keim-Malpass (2018) is a short data report, not a study of influence. It parses one quarter of Senate LDA XML (Q4 2009, just before the ACA) into eight pandas data frames. It sums reported dollars by umbrella issue code (Taxation $527.1M, Health $436.7M, with no denominator for the filing count) and finds 35 records whose Specific Issues text contains "pediatric". It runs no statistics. Its useful content is a list of data hazards:
- **Two series mixed:** the XML amount field does not separate in-house expenditures from outside-firm income.
- **Imprecise amounts:** expenses under $5,000 appear only as a checkbox, and income is rounded to the nearest $10,000.
- **Bundled issues:** one filing lists many issues, so dollars cannot be assigned to a single issue.
- **Filing time vs activity time:** files are grouped by when they were filed, so a quarter's files can carry activity from 2002 to 2008.

For Paul's systems, those hazards matter more than the results. Mentat's lobbying card and `sector_spend.py` now enforce the paper's main warning. They keep outside-firm fees and in-house expenses as two series and never add them (D-064, commit 914623152, which removed a double-counted $139.4M telecom total on 2026-10-09). `sector_spend.py` also assigns filings by activity period and keeps only the latest amendment.

The older LobbyView collector does not follow the same rule. Its per-side `amount_sum` and its top-spender `total_amount` add self-filer expenses and hired-firm income together. The brain's "ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M" figure probably comes from that mixed sum (UNVERIFIED). On issue codes, the collector correctly counts reports rather than dollars, which avoids the bundling trap that inflates the paper's own per-code dollar totals. The paper has nothing to say about networks, persuasion, legislators or elections.

bearings.paper_claim: LDA amount fields do not separate lobbying expenditures (in-house) from income (outside-firm fees), and nothing in the record links the two. Expenses under $5,000 are a checkbox with no amount, and income over $5,000 is rounded to the nearest $10,000. Reported dollars therefore cannot be split by type, and small spenders show no amount.
bearings.system_side: The LobbyView collector reads is_self_filer for each report. Its per-side, per-year amount_sum and finance_amount_sum, and its top-spender total_amount, still add every report's amount, whether self-filer expense or hired-firm income. Self-filer dollars are kept only as a sub-sum. Blank amounts are parsed as 0.0. The brain note records 'ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M' and 'self-filer = expense, hired firm = gross income'. A self-filer's expense figure already includes its payments to outside firms, so adding the outside firms' income for the same client counts those dollars twice. This is the double count that D-064 bans in sector_spend.py.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The hazard carries over directly: the LD-2 form semantics the paper describes still hold in the LobbyView vintage (2024-10-25). The paper's claim that the XML cannot separate the two series does not carry over: LobbyView exposes is_self_filer, so the system can split them and simply does not in these aggregates. Window: LobbyView reports for 1999-2024, with finance-joined coverage reliable through 2021. Two points are UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062): whether the brain's $228M ABA figure is the mixed total_amount, and how large the overlap is.

bearings.paper_claim: Pediatric issues sit in single filings alongside many unrelated issues (vaccines, Medicare/Medicaid, FDA, pandemic), so dollars cannot be assigned to one issue. Despite this, the paper reports dollar totals by umbrella code from a Filing x Issue merge: Taxation $527,147,333 and Health $436,651,121 for Q4 2009. No filing-count denominator is given.
bearings.system_side: For finance-joined reports, the collector counts reports per issue code (per_code += 1) and does not spread or repeat dollars across codes. The figure '322,473 issue-coded reports' is a report count.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies to any LDA source where one report carries several issue codes, so it holds for LobbyView and the Senate API alike. The paper's own per-code dollar totals probably count a bundled filing once per code. They show why the system's count-only design is right; they are not a benchmark to quote.

bearings.paper_claim: The amount data does not differentiate lobbying expenditures from income, so the analysis of dollar values is limited until the forms change.
bearings.system_side: Mentat's lobbying card reads sector_spend rows as two named series, hired_firms = income_total and in_house = expenses_total, and never adds them. sector_spend.py rejects combined keys such as income_plus_expenses and spend_total. The 2026-10-09 commit removed a summed telecom 2025 total ($139.4M), which now displays as $102.4M in-house and $37.0M in outside-firm fees.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence is a description of the federal LD-2 form, not an empirical estimate, so it carries over fully to 2021-2026 Senate LDA data. It supports the D-064 rule; it does not measure how large the overlap is.

bearings.paper_claim: LDA records are grouped by filing time, not activity time: Q4 2009 files contained activity from 2002-2008, and the authors had to filter to 2009 activity. They report no amendment handling.
bearings.system_side: sector_spend assigns each filing to its activity filing_year and filing_period, not to the date it was posted. Within each (registrant, client, filing_year, filing_period) group it keeps the latest parseable dt_posted, so an amendment replaces the original. A quarter counts as covered only after its LD-2 deadline (Apr 20, Jul 20, Oct 20, Jan 20) has passed by the producer's sweep date (D-130).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over: the same federal LDA filing structure applies. The system handles this hazard more strictly than the paper, which only date-filters and does not deduplicate amendments.

gaps_exposed: The LobbyView collector's spend aggregates (amount_sum, finance_amount_sum, top-spender total_amount) add self-filer expenses and hired-firm income. This contradicts the D-064 rule that sector_spend.py and Mentat now enforce. The ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M comparison in the brain may be a mixed figure. It should be re-derived as two separate series before it is quoted again.

Amounts reported only as the under-$5,000 checkbox are parsed as 0.0 in the LobbyView ingest, and income above $5,000 is rounded to the nearest $10,000. No receipt counts how many finance-side reports are affected. Small credit-union filers such as state leagues would be understated relative to large bank filers.

Neither Melange nor Mentat uses the Specific Issues free text. The paper proposes NLP and topic modeling on it as future work, and Kim et al. 2025 do the position-extraction version. The system's issue view is limited to issue codes and report counts.
flags: Do not quote the paper's per-code dollar totals (Taxation $527.1M, Health $436.7M) as benchmarks. They come from a Filing x Issue merge that probably counts a multi-issue filing's dollars under every code, they mix expenditure and income, and the paper gives no filing-count denominator.

Paul's positions list cites Harrison for mentat-fec-attribution.dedup-and-versions ('late-filed records'). The paper is about LDA filing-time vs activity-time grouping and says nothing about FEC amendment or memo versions, so the citation does not carry over to that component. The LDA analogue is already handled in sector_spend.py (activity-period assignment plus latest-dt_posted supersession).
Paul's positions list also cites Harrison for melange-legislative-data.congress-activity-score. The paper does not touch congress.gov bill data, so it has no bearing on that component.
The paper uses LDA dollars only as spend totals and builds no edges, so it raises no D-021 conflict. Any future reuse must keep LDA as an identity source, not an edge or weight source.
rel.paul_alignment: The evidence agrees with Paul's takeaway: the paper is an introductory walkthrough of an LDA pipeline (pandas, where to get the records, how to turn them into usable information), and its results are thin, with one quarter, one keyword and no statistics. His note that Kim's LobbyView is far larger also holds, and the system uses LobbyView as its historical source. His note misses where the paper's real value lies. Its stated limits (expenditures and income not separated, the under-$5,000 checkbox, $10,000 rounding, issue bundling, filing-time grouping) are the hazards the system has since ruled on: D-064 says never add the two series, D-130 sets the deadline-based quarter coverage rule, and the 10-09 commit removed the summed telecom figure. In that sense his note is out of date. It treats the paper as a how-to; the system now follows its warnings in Mentat and sector_spend.py but not yet in the LobbyView collector's spend aggregates.

related.why: LobbyView cleans and links the same LDA filings at full scale, which is the database Paul says supersedes Harrison. It also carries the is_self_filer field that makes the expenditure-vs-income split possible, the split Harrison says the raw XML lacks.
It does the text analysis that Harrison proposes as future work (Sec. 4), extracting positions from the specific-issue text of LDA reports.
Both use federal LDA filings; Bacik builds the multi-year lobbying network that Harrison's one-quarter parse never reaches.
Both rely on LDA spend fields, so the expenditure-vs-income semantics Harrison flags apply to Furnas's lobbying totals too.
Paul's own LDA disclosure report draws on the same LD-2 amounts, so the same caution about mixing the two series and about rounding applies.

paul_entries.citation: Harrison, Elizabeth, et al. “An application of data mining techniques to explore congressional lobbying records for patterns in pediatric special interest expenditures prior to the Affordable Care Act.” *Frontiers in Big Data*, vol. 1, 20 Aug. 2018, [https://doi.org/10.3389/fdata.2018.00003](https://doi.org/10.3389/fdata.2018.00003).
paul_entries.text:
Harrison, Elizabeth, et al. “An application of data mining techniques to explore congressional lobbying records for patterns in pediatric special interest expenditures prior to the Affordable Care Act.” *Frontiers in Big Data*, vol. 1, 20 Aug. 2018, [https://doi.org/10.3389/fdata.2018.00003](https://doi.org/10.3389/fdata.2018.00003).

This article by professors from the University of Virginia, Charlottesville explores the use of data-mining in lobbying records to measure the influence of special interest groups in the legislative process of congressional bills, most notably with the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare). It provides a cursory study into how to construct the models necessary for the pipelining of such information, through the use of Python pandas, where to obtain such information, such as the LDA, and how to transform said data into actionable information. It is relatively important to the current research in that it provides a foundational basis for the processing of such data and the do’s and don’ts of such methods. However, the results from this data are lack-luster and this is likely a result of the authors limitations in-regards to their technical ability, and other articles, such as Professor Kim’s, provide a database of a far greater magnitude. Still, for an introductory overview of the pipelining of such data, this article proves adequate.
